title: Stat 3125 ProjectGuide
text:
This website exists as a resource for STAT 3125 students looking to create a semester project with the intention of presenting at Analytics Day, fulfilling an honors contract, or simply expanding their portfolio.
Resources available on this site include but are not limited to:

Where to find your dataset
Using popular R packages to make data analysis easier
Performing Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
Possible data processing/modeling methods
Using ggplot2 for easy plot creation
Assembling a presentation/poster

If this is your first time using the site, it is recommended to begin by reading our Getting Started page, which will prepare you for your upcoming project.

title: Getting Started
text:
Before a student can get underway with a project, there are a few pieces of prerequisite knowledge that are recommended to prevent roadblocks further down the line.

R and R Studio: The first couple weeks of class will ensure that you are set up with this software, as it is required for classwork. The guides on this website are written with R users in mind.
Popular R packages: These packages will make appearances in some of the example projects on this site and greatly simplify the work of data analysis and visualization.

An Introduction to finalfit
text:
Introduction
For Project A, The student utilized the finalfit package to create clean tables for their logistic regression model. finalfit is an open-source package to be used with R Studio to create clean, publication-ready tables for the data analysis model of your choosing. The package compiles your numbers into a table, grouping data in an efficient, automated way to present in a paper or poster. finalfit is a great programming package for beginners in data analytics research.


Use Cases and Limitations



finalfit Can:

Summarize quantitative variable values by a categorical variable
Summarize regression model results in table format
Summarize regression model results into a plot






finalfit Cannot:

Analyze results from advanced machine learning models
Handle large amounts of levels for categorical variables
Perform Bayesian modeling

title: Choosing Your Question
text: When choosing your research question, it’s important to look at all your different variables and determine what you would like to assess. Pick something that is meaningful to you, you can connect with, or something that genuinely interests you. When I first started this project, I scrolled through the dataset and looked at all the different variables and numbers. There’s many to choose from, so you’ll want to narrow it down significantly. Try not to get overwhelmed and lost in all the numbers – take this time to gather ideas. Upon looking through the dataset, I thought about what I might want to investigate or what story I want to tell. I have an interest in healthcare deserts and mental health, so it made sense to look at opioid misuse in rural populations in people with and without mental health disorders. I was able to further narrow this down to looking at young adults in the south as my sample. This decision allowed for me to have more connection with this analysis as I could fall into these categories based on my age and where I live. Overall, the important thing to remember when choosing your question is to think about the story you want to tell using the data you are given.

title: An Introduction to dplyr
text:
Introduction
Per its website, dplyr is “a grammar of data manipulation” that greatly simplifies data processing using core verbiage such as:

group_by(): subdivides datasets for independent analysis
filter(): removes values that do not match a given condition
mutate(): creates new variables from existing ones
summarize(): aggregates data from multiple values into a single summary value
select(): selects (or deselects) variables to include or exclude from the dataset



Improvements over base R
While dplyr’s data manipulation features do not enable the user to perform any actions that aren’t possible in base R, its simplicity is its key. dplyr allows users to transform their datasets in simple commands rather than nested function calls. The following table from the official dplyr <-> base R article demonstrates the reduction in complexity that dplyr functions enable.







dplyr
base




arrange(df, x)
df[order(x), , drop = FALSE]


distinct(df, x)
df[!duplicated(x), , drop = FALSE], unique()


filter(df, x)
df[which(x), , drop = FALSE], subset()


mutate(df, z = x + y)
df$z <- df$x + df$y, transform()


pull(df, 1)
df[[1]]


pull(df, x)
df$x


rename(df, y = x)
names(df)[names(df) == "x"] <- "y"


relocate(df, y)
df[union("y", names(df))]


select(df, x, y)
df[c("x", "y")], subset()


select(df, starts_with("x"))
df[grep("^x", names(df))]


summarise(df, mean(x))
mean(df$x), tapply(), aggregate(), by()


slice(df, c(1, 2, 5))
df[c(1, 2, 5), , drop = FALSE]



In addition to reducing individual calls, some dplyr functions would require multiple separate calls in base R to achieve the same result. For example, let’s examine the iris dataset, a staple resource in data science education, and attempt to tally the number of flowers of each species in the dataset. In dplyr, all we would have to do is:

library(dplyr)
data <- iris %>%
group_by(Species) %>%
summarize(mean_sepal_width = mean(Sepal.Width)) %>%
print()

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Species    mean_sepal_width
  <fct>                 <dbl>
1 setosa                 3.43
2 versicolor             2.77
3 virginica              2.97


The equivalent code in base R would look something like this:

means <- tapply(iris$Sepal.Width, iris$Species, mean)
data <- data.frame(
  Species = names(means),
  mean_sepal_width = as.vector(means),
  row.names = NULL
)
print(data)

     Species mean_sepal_width
1     setosa            3.428
2 versicolor            2.770
3  virginica            2.974


Note how dplyr avoids repeat references as well as intermediary variables. These are some of the many reasons data scientists prefer dplyr for R data manipulation.


A Note on Pipes in R
If characters such as %>% or |> look unfamiliar to you, that may be because you’ve never worked with R’s pipe system before. Put simply, pipes are simple operators that allow programmers to chain functions to each other using common data, reducing redundant object references and simplifying code.
For example, let’s look at the code below (once again using the iris dataset), where the user is attempting to calculate how the average sepal width of setosa and versicolor flowers compare.

Base Code

library(dplyr)
data <- iris
data <- filter(data, Species %in% c("setosa", "versicolor"))
data <- group_by(data, Species)
data <- summarize(data, mean_sepal_width = mean(Sepal.Width))
print(data)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Species    mean_sepal_width
  <fct>                 <dbl>
1 setosa                 3.43
2 versicolor             2.77




Using Pipes

library(dplyr)
data <- iris %>%
  filter(Species %in% c("setosa", "versicolor")) %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarize(mean_sepal_width = mean(Sepal.Width)) %>%
  print()

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Species    mean_sepal_width
  <fct>                 <dbl>
1 setosa                 3.43
2 versicolor             2.77


When you use pipes, the object and its variables are preserved between operations, making references much more intuitive and code less cluttered. It can take a bit to adjust, but once you get comfortable using pipes it will make your R coding much easier.

title: Finding a Dataset
text:
The first step in developing a project in data science is finding a dataset to analyze. Students may pursue a variety of avenues when sourcing their data, and the below sections serve to highlight some of the most popular and extensive free data hubs on the internet.

Data.gov
Data.gov is the US government’s central host for public data, containing over 500,000 datasets as of 2026. Most relevant to Stat 3125 students, the site hosts nearly 20,000 datasets from the Department of Health & Human Services, with most popular datasets including:

U.S. Chronic Disease Indicators (Last updated 6/4/2026)
NCHS - Leading Causes of Death: United States (Last updated 4/21/2025)
Mental Health Care in the Last 4 Weeks (Last updated 4/21/2025)

In addition, the Center for Disease Control (CDC) hosts its own portal for open data, available at data.cdc.gov. The site hosts over 1,500 datasets, including many key data sources covering the COVID-19 pandemic.


Kaggle
Kaggle is a privately-run platform for datasets and data science competitions. Users are free to publish their own data sets and respond to others with their own analysis. Nearly any topic of dataset can be found on Kaggle, from sports to disease to animal species. The key drawback of Kaggle is that the public nature of its data can make it difficult to find quality datasets at times.


Google Dataset Search
Google Dataset Search is a search tool built on the foundations of Google Research that aggregates public datasets from across the internet into a searchable site. Details included in searches include:

Data source
Data format
Date last updated
Description
Governing body (when applicable)

Google Dataset Search is a good resource for students who know the topic they want to cover but want a wholistic picture of possible data sources.
